The EPR spectrum of a free radical, like the 13C-labelled methyl radical (13CH3•), is determined by the number of equivalent hyperfine interactions. In this case, the methyl radical has three equivalent hydrogen atoms, which are the only source of hyperfine interactions.

For a free radical with one unpaired electron, the EPR spectrum will have a pattern of lines that correspond to the possible combinations of spin states of the unpaired electron and the hyperfine interactions. The number of lines in the spectrum is determined by the number of equivalent hyperfine interactions.

For a methyl radical, there are three equivalent hydrogen atoms, which means there are three possible hyperfine interactions. However, since the hyperfine interactions are equivalent, they will all contribute the same amount to the energy levels, resulting in a single line for each spin state (up and down) of the unpaired electron.

Therefore, the EPR spectrum of a solution of 13C-labelled methyl radical (13CH3•) will have two lines, one for each spin state of the unpaired electron.
